title: The affine-target extension locus on a factorial scheme has Cartier complement
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $W$ be a nonempty integral $k$-scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme] which is Noetherian, meaning locally Noetherian [pqf-def-locnoeth] and quasi-compact [def-weil-pbc-quasi-compact-scheme]. Suppose each local ring $\mathcal O_{W,w}$ is a unique factorization domain, meaning a domain in which every nonzero nonunit has a factorization into prime elements unique up to units and order. Let $A$ be a finitely generated commutative $k$-algebra, let $T=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], let $H\subseteq W$ be a dense open subscheme, and let $h:H\to T$ be a $k$-morphism. Define
$$E=\bigcup\{V\subseteq W\text{ open}:\ \exists h_V:V\to T\text{ over }k,\ h_V|_{V\cap H}=h|_{V\cap H}\}.$$
There exists an effective Cartier divisor $P\subset W$ [def-pc-divisor-line-bundle], possibly empty, whose underlying closed subset is exactly $W\setminus E$. Here effective Cartier means that the defining ideal is locally generated by a non-zero-divisor. No properness of $T$ is assumed.

source.place: Chapter I, proof of Lemma 3.3, printed pp.17–18, polar-divisor argument, applied to finitely many affine coordinates. Supporting source: literature/stacks-project/divisors.tex, Tag 0AGA, lemma-weil-divisor-is-cartier-UFD. The Cartier complement is the union of the negative supports of the coordinate divisors; the local denominator argument is in the report.

proof.text: Choose a generic point $\eta$ of the nonempty integral scheme $W$ using [lem-sc-scheme-sober], and put $K=\mathcal O_{W,\eta}$. By [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field], sections on nonempty opens and all local rings inject compatibly into $K$, and $K$ is the fraction field of each local ring. Choose algebra generators $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ of $A$ over $k$, allowing $n=0$. The affine adjunction [lem-a1-locally-ringed-space-affine-adjunction] sends $h$ to $A\to\Gamma(H,\mathcal O_H)$. Composing with the generic germ gives a $k$-algebra map $\phi:A\to K$; put $f_i=\phi(a_i)$. Here $\eta\in H$ since $H$ is nonempty open in an integral scheme.

source.place: Tag 01RV, lemma-integral-scheme-rational-functions; Schemes Tag 01I1, lemma-morphism-into-affine; Milne AV I, proof of Lemma 3.3, pp.17–18, rational functions in the target local ring

proof.text: For $w\in W$, we claim $w\in E$ if and only if every $f_i$ belongs to $\mathcal O_{W,w}\subset K$. An extension on a neighbourhood $V$ of $w$ gives this inclusion by taking coordinate germs: its generic map equals $\phi$, because $V\cap H$ contains $\eta$. Conversely, represent the finitely many local elements $f_i$ by sections $s_i$ on a common neighbourhood $V$ of $w$, using [def-weil-pbc-module-stalk]. Evaluate polynomials to obtain $k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\to\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)$. Every relation in the kernel of $k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\twoheadrightarrow A$ maps to zero in $K$ under $X_i\mapsto f_i$, hence is zero as a section by [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field]. Thus this map factors through $A$. The natural bijection [lem-a1-locally-ringed-space-affine-adjunction] gives a $k$-morphism $h_V:V\to T$; naturality with respect to $k\to A$ checks that it is over $k$. On $V\cap H$, its coordinate sections equal those of $h$ by their identical generic germs and the same injectivity. The adjunction then gives equality of the restricted morphisms. This is exactly the extension required in the definition of $E$. The empty coordinate family gives the structural map when $A=k$.

source.place: Tag 01I1, lemma-morphism-into-affine, and Example 01JH, example-global-sections; explicit finite-coordinate version of the local-ring test in Milne AV I, proof of Lemma 3.3

proof.text: For each $i$ define an ideal subsheaf $\mathcal D_i\subset\mathcal O_W$ by $\mathcal D_i(V)=\{c\in\mathcal O_W(V):cf_i\text{ is represented by a section on }V\}$ for nonempty $V$, interpreting products in $K$. It is a sheaf: local representatives of $cf_i$ agree on nonempty overlaps by [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field], and glue by the structure-sheaf axiom. If $f_i=0$, then $\mathcal D_i=\mathcal O_W$. If $f_i\ne0$, take a nonempty affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$. By [lem-sc-integral-function-field-affine-fraction], write $f_i=a/b$ in $K$, with $a,b\in R$ nonzero. Their germs are nonzero in every stalk of $U$, by the injection into $K$, and are therefore nonzerodivisors. By [def-sc-meromorphic-module], $a/b$ is a meromorphic section on $U$ with inverse $b/a$; multiplication by it is an isomorphism, in particular injective. Apply [lem-sc-hilbert-denominator-ideal-nowhere-dense] on $U$ with $\mathcal L=\mathcal O_U$ and this regular meromorphic section: its denominator ideal is quasi-coherent. It equals $\mathcal D_i|_U$: fractions map injectively to $K$ (a zero generic fraction has zero numerator), and this remains true after sheafification by local representatives. Thus equality with a regular section can be tested in $K$. Quasi-coherence is local on affine opens, so each $\mathcal D_i$ is quasi-coherent on $W$. No assertion about a zero section is taken from the regular-meromorphic-section theorem.

source.place: Tag 02P0, lemma-regular-meromorphic-ideal-denominators, statement and affine proof; Tags 01X2/01X4, meromorphic sections; applied to the nonzero coordinate functions only

proof.text: For every $w$, the stalk of this ideal is exactly $\mathcal D_{i,w}=\{c\in\mathcal O_{W,w}:cf_i\in\mathcal O_{W,w}\}$ inside $K$. One inclusion follows by taking germs of the defining regular sections. For the converse choose section representatives near $w$ of $c$ and of $cf_i$ using [def-weil-pbc-module-stalk]; on their common neighbourhood their equality in $K$ says precisely that the representative of $c$ belongs to $\mathcal D_i$. Taking its germ proves the other inclusion. In particular $\mathcal D_{i,w}=\mathcal O_{W,w}$ if and only if $f_i\in\mathcal O_{W,w}$ (test $c=1$). The injections used here are those of [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field].

source.place: Tag 02P0, lemma-regular-meromorphic-ideal-denominators, affine localization calculation, expanded at a stalk

proof.text: Fix $w$ and write $B=\mathcal O_{W,w}$. If $f_i=0$ take $b_i=1$. Otherwise write $f_i=u_i/b_i$ in its fraction field $K$, canceling the common prime factors of numerator and denominator using the assumed unique factorization in $B$; thus $u_i,b_i\ne0$ have no common prime factor. For $c\in B$, membership $cf_i\in B$ is equivalent to $b_i\mid cu_i$. Prime factorization shows this is equivalent to $b_i\mid c$: for each prime factor of $b_i$, its exponent in $u_i$ is zero, so its whole exponent must occur in $c$. For $c=0$ both divisibilities hold. Conversely $c=b_id$ gives $cf_i=du_i$. Step 4 therefore gives $\mathcal D_{i,w}=(b_i)$ with $b_i\ne0$. This is only a local choice; no affine coordinate ring is assumed to be a UFD.

source.place: Chapter I, proof of Lemma 3.3, pp.17–18, polar-divisor/local-ring criterion, expanded by prime-factor cancellation; compare Stacks Tag 0AGA, lemma-weil-divisor-is-cartier-UFD

proof.text: Form $\mathcal J=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathcal D_i$, the quasi-coherent ideal product of [def-sbc-ideal-sheaf-powers], taking $\mathcal J=\mathcal O_W$ if $n=0$. At a stalk this product is the product of the stalk ideals. Take an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$ containing $w$, with prime $\mathfrak p_w$. Each $\mathcal D_i$ is quasi-coherent (step 3), so $\mathcal D_i|_U=\mathcal D_i(U)^\sim$, and by [def-sbc-ideal-sheaf-powers] $\mathcal J|_U=(\mathcal D_1(U)\cdots\mathcal D_n(U))^\sim$. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-tilde-stalk-localization] the stalk of an ideal $I^\sim$ at $w$ is $I_{\mathfrak p_w}\subseteq R_{\mathfrak p_w}=\mathcal O_{W,w}$, with germs [def-weil-pbc-module-stalk] corresponding to fractions. Hence $\mathcal J_w=(\mathcal D_1(U)\cdots\mathcal D_n(U))_{\mathfrak p_w}=\prod_i\mathcal D_i(U)_{\mathfrak p_w}=\prod_i\mathcal D_{i,w}$, since localization commutes with finite products of ideals (a product of fractions $x_i/s_i$ is $(\prod x_i)/(\prod s_i)$, and conversely $x/s$ with $x=\sum_j\prod_i x_{ij}$ is $\sum_j (x_{1j}/s)\prod_{i\ge2}(x_{ij}/1)$). Hence step 5 gives $\mathcal J_w=(\prod_i b_i)$. The product is nonzero in the domain $\mathcal O_{W,w}$, including the empty product $1$, so it is a nonzerodivisor. The construction [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-coherent-ideal-closed-subscheme] supplies a closed subscheme $P\hookrightarrow W$ with ideal $\mathcal J$. Apply [lem-sfb-stalk-nonzerodivisor-cartier-spreading] to this closed subscheme: $W$ is locally Noetherian by hypothesis, and its ideal has a nonzerodivisor generator at every stalk. Thus $P$ is an effective Cartier divisor, in the sense of [def-pc-divisor-line-bundle].

source.place: Tag 0AG8, lemma-effective-Cartier-in-points (2); Schemes Tags 01HM and 01IN, closed subscheme of a quasi-coherent ideal; finite products give the union of polar supports

proof.text:
We check the underlying set, including the empty case. On an affine neighbourhood $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$, the closed subscheme construction [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-coherent-ideal-closed-subscheme] identifies $P\cap U$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(R/\mathcal J(U))$. Thus $w
otin|P|$ exactly when $\mathcal J(U)
ot\subseteq\mathfrak p_w$, equivalently $\mathcal J_w=\mathcal O_{W,w}$ by the localization description [lem-weil-pbc-spec-tilde-stalk-localization]. Explicitly an element outside $\mathfrak p_w$ becomes a unit; conversely if the localized ideal contains $1$, combining its finitely many fractions gives a numerator in the ideal outside $\mathfrak p_w$. Since $\mathcal J_w=(\prod_i b_i)$, it is the unit ideal exactly when every $b_i$ is a unit: if $v\prod_i b_i=1$, then $v\prod_{j
e i}b_j$ is an inverse of $b_i$, and the reverse implication follows by multiplying inverses. By steps 4–5 this is equivalent to every $f_i$ being in $\mathcal O_{W,w}$, hence by step 2 to $w\in E$. Therefore $|P|=W\setminus E$. If there are no generators, or all coordinates are regular everywhere, all the denominator ideals are unit ideals, $\mathcal J=\mathcal O_W$, and $P$ is empty, as allowed. The argument never assumes $T$ proper.
